title: Can, can't, may, must
title_target: 할 수 있어요 — Hal su isseoyo
goal: Express ability, permission and obligation — and turn things down without offending anyone, which in Korea matters as much as the grammar itself.
bekal: expressing ability with -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 and -(으)ㄹ 수 없어요
telling 못 apart from 안 and from -지 않아요
asking for and giving permission with -아도/어도 돼요

dialogs.title: 대화 — Saying no without hurting
dialogs.intro: Suji invites Ani to a party. Notice that Ani never once says the word "no", and her refusal is still perfectly clear.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Ani, can you come to the party on Friday?
lines.literal: Ani — Ms., Friday-on — party — go-will — possibility — exists?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Friday? Just a second… ah, Friday is a bit difficult.
lines.literal: Friday — polite? just-a-moment — polite… ah, Friday — as-for — a-little — difficult.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Why? Do you have something on?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Yes, I have to work that evening. So I can't come.
lines.literal: yes, evening-in — work-must — becomes. so — can't — go.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Ah, that's a shame. How about Saturday?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Saturday works! What time should I come?
lines.literal: Saturday — as-for — fine! what — hour-at — go-must — becomes?

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Seven. It's fine to come late.
lines.literal: seven — o'clock — polite. late — come-even-if — okay.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: You don't need to bring anything. Just come.
lines.literal: anything — not — bring-come-even-if — okay. just-so — come.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: OK. Oh, I can't drink alcohol. Is that all right?
lines.literal: understood. ah, I — as-for — alcohol — object — can't — drink. okay?

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Of course it's all right. It's fine not to drink.

notes: **Saying no directly is very rare in Korean.** Notice that Ani never says 안 가요. What she uses is 좀 어려워요 ("it's a bit difficult") — and it's fully understood as a refusal. The same goes for 좀 힘들어요 and 다음에 할게요. Refusing with a flat 안 돼요 sounds sharp except between close friends.
**좀 shows up again as a softener.** 어려워요 on its own sounds like a firm statement; 좀 어려워요 sounds like a gentle apology. When declining, 좀 is practically required.

**못 goes before the verb and expresses an outside obstacle.** 술을 못 마셔요 means "I can't drink" — your body can't take it, your religion forbids it, or you're on medication. If Ani said 술을 안 마셔요, it would mean "I choose not to drink". In Korea, where invitations to drink are part of social life, the difference is very useful.
**못 is pronounced *mon* before ㅁ and ㄴ.** 못 마셔요 is read *mon masyeoyo*, not *mot masyeoyo* — the nasal assimilation rule explained at the front of the book.

**아쉬워요 means "what a shame".** It isn't sadness but a light sense of a missed chance — used when plans fall through, when a holiday ends, when a friend moves away. One of the words Koreans use most and textbooks teach least.
**당연히 means "of course".** It answers a question whose answer is obvious, while reassuring the other person there's nothing to worry about. The casual equivalent is 그럼요.
**-아도/어도 돼요 is used both to ask for and to give permission.** 늦게 와도 돼요? = may I come late? 늦게 와도 돼요. = it's fine to come late. Exactly the same form, told apart by the intonation at the end.

**아무것도 안 가져와도 돼요 uses two negatives at once** and still means something positive: "it's fine not to bring anything". Stacked structures like this feel heavy at first — read them from the inside out: 안 가져오다 (not bring) + -아도 되다 (it's OK) = it's OK not to bring.

grammars.title: -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 / 없어요 — can and can't
body: Literally "there is / there is no way to…". 수 is a noun meaning "way, possibility", which is why it pairs with 있다/없다.
after: **The form is exactly like the -(으)ㄹ 거예요 you just learned** — ㄹ for vowel stems, 을 for consonant stems. Master one and you get every -(으)ㄹ-based form for free.
**-(으)ㄹ 수 없어요 and 못 mean the same, with a different tone.** 갈 수 없어요 is more written and more neutral; 못 가요 is more spoken and shorter. In everyday conversation, 못 is far more common.

grammars.title: Permission and obligation
body: Two patterns built from the 해요 form you already have. Drop 요, then attach.
after: ⚠️ **"Must not" and "don't have to" are two completely different things, and the forms are easy to mix up** — just as in English. 가면 안 돼요 = you're not allowed to go. 안 가도 돼요 = you don't have to go. Swapping them can turn a ban into a let-off, or the other way round.
**돼요 and 해요 in the obligation form are the same.** 가야 돼요 is a bit more spoken, 가야 해요 a bit more written. Use either.

**되다 on its own means "become, be allowed, work out".** 돼요? = is that OK? can I? 안 돼요 = no, you can't, it's not happening. One of the most versatile words in Korean, and you'll hear it dozens of times a day.

grammars.title: Three ways to say no, one table
body: All of them have already appeared in this book. This page puts them in order.
after: ⚠️ **하다 verbs split apart with 안 and 못.** 공부 **안** 해요, 공부 **못** 해요 — not 안 공부해요. But the -지 않다 form doesn't split: 공부하지 않아요.
For everyday use, **안 and 못 are enough**. Just recognize the other two so you understand them when you read them.

blocks.text: In Korea, how you refuse matters more than what you refuse. Every sentence below means "no", yet none of them sounds like it — and that's exactly what makes them usable.

head: Sentence
Literal meaning
What it really means
rows: No, but I feel bad saying so.
A polite excuse that needs no explanation.
A direct but still polite refusal.

blocks.text: Notice that almost all of them end with a vague reason — on purpose. Explaining your refusal in detail is actually seen as too much; a Korean listener won't press.

blocks.title: 술 and how to turn it down
items: Invitations to drink are a big part of social and working life in Korea, and declining takes the right sentence.
**저는 술을 못 마셔요** ("I can't drink") is accepted far more easily than 안 마셔요 ("I don't drink"), because it points to an obstacle, not a choice. Religious, health or medication reasons all fit under 못.
You can offer to have 사이다 (clear soda) instead — and pouring drinks for others, whatever is in the glass, still makes you part of it.
⚠️ Pouring your own drink is considered impolite at a Korean table; people pour for each other. Hold the bottle with both hands when pouring for someone older.

exercises.prompt: Change into the ability form with -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요.

items: 저는 술을 ____ 마셔요. It's for health reasons.
고기를 ____ 먹어요. I simply don't want to.
오늘 공부 ____ 했어요. I was lazy.
You don't need to bring anything.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: 금요일에 갈 수 있어요? — 금요일은 좀 어려워요. — 일해야 돼요. — 늦게 와도 돼요. — 아무것도 안 가져와도 돼요. — 저는 술을 못 마셔요.
금요일에 갈 수 있어요? — 저녁에 일해야 돼요. — 늦게 와도 돼요. — 금요일은 좀 어려워요. — 저는 술을 못 마셔요.
